questions.scenario: A developer-tools company runs an automated PR reviewer over the Messages API. One of its checks is phrased "Check that code comments are accurate." Developers report that 70% of the comment-related findings are about wording, missing punctuation, outdated TODO owners, or comments that "could be clearer," and they have started ignoring the reviewer. Yet the team had two incidents where a comment claimed a function was idempotent when the code wasn't, and that is exactly the class of problem they want caught. What is the most effective change to this check?
options: Rephrase it to flag a comment only when the behavior it claims contradicts what the code actually does, and to skip wording, style and TODO metadata.
Keep the check but add "only report comment issues you are highly confident about", so that low-value wording findings get filtered out.
Have the reviewer score each comment finding from 1 to 10, and post only the findings scored 8 or higher on the pull request.
Turn the comment check off entirely, since its false positives are hurting trust in the reviewer's other, more accurate checks.
questions.why_correct: El criterio vago ('que sean precisos') deja al modelo decidir qué cuenta, y elige estilo. Definir explícitamente qué entra (un comentario que contradice el comportamiento real del código) y qué no (redacción, estilo, TODOs) apunta justo al tipo de bug que causó los incidentes.

why_wrong.1: La guía lo dice: 'solo alta confianza' no mejora la precisión frente a criterios categóricos concretos. El modelo puede estar muy seguro de que falta una coma.
why_wrong.2: Es filtrado por confianza autoinformada: está mal calibrada y no cambia qué *categoría* de problema se busca.
why_wrong.3: Recuperás confianza pero perdés exactamente los hallazgos que el equipo necesita (el comentario de idempotencia).

questions.rule: Criterio vago → decide el modelo. Escribí qué se reporta y qué se saltea, por categoría.
questions.source_quote: The importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions (e.g., "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior" vs "check that comments are accurate")

questions.scenario: A fintech's review bot classifies each finding as `critical`, `major` or `minor` through an enum in a strict tool schema. The prompt defines the levels as "critical: serious problems; major: significant problems; minor: small problems." An audit of 500 findings shows the same kind of issue landing in different buckets across PRs: an unchecked `null` from the payments API was `critical` in one PR and `minor` in another, and only `critical` findings page the on-call engineer. The enum is enforced and every output is schema-valid. What is the most effective change?
options: Add a fourth enum value, `blocker`, above `critical`, so the most dangerous issues get their own bucket and stop being mixed with the rest.
Run each review three times and assign the severity chosen by the majority, so that one-off misclassifications are voted out.
Ask the model to include a confidence score with each severity, and page on-call only for critical findings with high confidence.
Define each severity with explicit criteria and a concrete code example per level, such as an unchecked null from a payments response being critical.
questions.why_correct: El enum garantiza que el valor sea uno de los tres, no qué *significa* cada uno. Con definiciones vagas ('serio', 'significativo') cada corrida interpreta distinto. Criterios explícitos más un ejemplo de código por nivel fijan la frontera y la clasificación se vuelve consistente.

why_wrong.0: Más buckets con las mismas definiciones vagas suman otra frontera ambigua.
why_wrong.1: Triplica el costo y solo promedia la ambigüedad: si el criterio es vago, la mayoría también puede estar equivocada.
why_wrong.2: Suma un número mal calibrado encima de una clasificación inconsistente; sigue sin definir qué es critical.

questions.rule: Severidad consistente = criterios explícitos + un ejemplo de código por nivel. El enum solo garantiza la forma.
questions.source_quote: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification

questions.scenario: A subscription retailer's support agent writes a structured summary after each chat, with the fields `issue_type`, `resolution` and `churn_risk` (`low`/`medium`/`high`). The retention team calls every customer rated `high`. An audit of 800 chats found that `churn_risk` matched actual cancellations only 31% of the time; the model inferred it from tone, emojis or the number of messages. Meanwhile, some customers who wrote "I want to cancel" were rated `medium`. The other fields are accurate. Retention still needs a reliable trigger for its outreach calls. What is the most effective change?
options: Add few-shot examples of high, medium and low churn-risk chats, so the model learns which tones and message patterns predict a cancellation.
Replace `churn_risk` with a `cancellation_requested` boolean defined explicitly: true only when the customer states an intent to cancel or downgrade.
Keep `churn_risk` but add a `confidence` field, and call only the customers rated `high` with a confidence above 0.8 to reduce wasted calls.
Add an instruction to be careful and conservative when rating churn risk, and to choose `medium` whenever the signals in the chat are mixed.
questions.why_correct: Predecir churn por el tono es una categoría donde el modelo no es confiable (31%). En vez de seguir pidiéndola, se reemplaza por algo con frontera explícita y verificable en el texto: ¿el cliente dijo que quiere cancelar o bajar de plan? Retention recibe un disparador confiable.

why_wrong.0: Le enseña a adivinar mejor algo que no está en el texto; el dato que importa (pidió cancelar) no depende del tono.
why_wrong.2: La confianza autoinformada sobre una inferencia poco confiable no la vuelve confiable, y los 'I want to cancel' en `medium` siguen escapando.
why_wrong.3: Vago: 'conservador' empuja todo a `medium`, incluidos los que pidieron cancelar.

questions.rule: Categoría donde el modelo no es confiable → sacala o reemplazala por un criterio explícito y verificable.
questions.source_quote: Be specific about the output format and constraints you want.

questions.scenario: A consulting firm's research system has a synthesis subagent that writes market briefs from findings returned by search subagents. The coordinator tells it: "Focus on high-quality, recent sources." Client reviews found that 22% of cited claims came from vendor press releases, forum posts, or reports older than 2022, all of which the firm's methodology excludes, while some recent government statistics were dropped as "less relevant." Clients have also asked to see what was left out of each brief and why. What is the most effective change to the subagent's instructions?
options: Ask the subagent to rate each source's quality from 1 to 5 and to include only the sources rated 4 or 5 in the final brief.
Replace the instruction with "Use only the most authoritative and up-to-date sources available", written at the top of the subagent's prompt.
Define explicit inclusion criteria (allowed source types, published 2022 or later) and exclusion criteria, and list each excluded source with the rule it failed.
Remove all sources older than 2022 in code before synthesis, and keep the current instruction for judging which of the remaining sources are high-quality.
questions.why_correct: 'Alta calidad, reciente' deja al modelo decidir, y decide distinto que la metodología. Criterios explícitos de inclusión (tipos de fuente, desde 2022) y de exclusión, más la lista de fuentes excluidas con la regla que no cumplieron, alinean el resultado y le dan al cliente la trazabilidad que pidió.

why_wrong.0: Un puntaje de 1 a 5 sin definición es otro criterio vago, con filtrado por confianza encima.
why_wrong.1: Cambiar un adjetivo vago por otro ('autoritativo') no define la frontera.
why_wrong.3: Casi: el filtro por fecha en código es determinístico y está bien, pero los tipos de fuente (press releases, foros) siguen librados a 'alta calidad', y no hay lista de excluidas.

questions.rule: Fronteras explícitas de inclusión y exclusión, y lo excluido listado con su motivo.
questions.source_quote: Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions. Being specific about the output you want can help enhance results.

questions.scenario: A legal-ops team extracts an `obligations` array from supplier contracts with structured outputs; each item has `party`, `action` and `deadline`. The prompt says "Extract all obligations." Precision is 42%: the array fills up with definitions ("'Services' means..."), recitals ("WHEREAS the Supplier..."), permissions ("The Customer may terminate..."), and governing-law boilerplate. Recall on real obligations is fine. Lawyers want a list they can rely on without re-reading the contract, and some genuine obligations are phrased with "agrees to" or "will" rather than "shall". What is the most effective change?
options: Define what counts: a party committed to an action ("shall", "must", "agrees to", "will"), and what doesn't: definitions, recitals, permissions with "may", and boilerplate.
Post-filter the array in code, keeping only items whose source sentence contains "shall" or "must", and drop the rest before lawyers see the list.
Change the instruction to "Extract only the important obligations" so the model leaves out minor clauses and boilerplate on its own.
Add an `is_obligation` boolean and a `confidence` score to each item, and show lawyers only the items marked true with confidence above 0.9.
questions.why_correct: 'Todas las obligaciones' es una frontera vaga y el modelo la estira. Definir qué entra (un compromiso de una parte, con sus formas reales: shall, must, agrees to, will) y qué queda afuera (definiciones, considerandos, permisos con 'may', boilerplate) sube la precisión sin perder las obligaciones redactadas distinto.

why_wrong.1: Determinístico pero ciego: tira las obligaciones con 'agrees to' o 'will', que el equipo sabe que existen.
why_wrong.2: 'Importantes' es todavía más vago: cambia una frontera difusa por otra y puede bajar el recall.
why_wrong.3: Filtrar por confianza autoinformada no define qué es una obligación; el modelo puede estar muy seguro de que un considerando lo es.

questions.rule: Precisión baja en una extracción → definí explícitamente qué entra y qué queda afuera, con las variantes reales.
questions.source_quote: Writing specific review criteria that define which issues to report (bugs, security) versus skip (minor style, local patterns) rather than relying on confidence-based filtering

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company's automated reviewer reports four categories: security, correctness, performance and accessibility. Over the last month, accessibility findings had a 68% false-positive rate (flagging decorative images and ARIA patterns that the design system already handles), while security and correctness stayed above 90% precision. Developer surveys show people now dismiss the reviewer's comments wholesale, and a real authorization bug was merged after its finding was ignored. The team believes accessibility checks are valuable in the long term, but it needs developer trust back this sprint. What should the team do first?
options: Add "Only report accessibility issues when you are highly confident" to the prompt, and keep all four categories active while monitoring results.
Raise the bar for every category so the reviewer posts fewer comments overall, and developers see less noise on each pull request.
Temporarily stop posting accessibility findings, and improve that category's criteria offline against labeled examples before turning it back on.
Move accessibility findings into a collapsed "Other" section at the bottom of each review, so they stay visible without competing with security.
questions.why_correct: Una categoría con muchos falsos positivos arrastra la confianza en las categorías buenas (se ignoró un bug real de autorización). La guía indica desactivarla temporalmente para recuperar la confianza mientras se mejoran sus criterios, y recién después volver a activarla.

why_wrong.0: 'Solo con alta confianza' es el tipo de instrucción general que la guía dice que no mejora la precisión.
why_wrong.1: Recorta también security y correctness, que andaban bien: bajás el ruido perdiendo justo lo valioso.
why_wrong.3: Sigue publicando un 68% de ruido; colapsado o no, el reviewer sigue diciendo cosas falsas y la confianza no vuelve.

questions.rule: Categoría con muchos falsos positivos que mata la confianza → apagala temporalmente y mejorá sus criterios aparte.
questions.source_quote: Temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while improving prompts for those categories

questions.scenario: A payments company runs a secrets scan in CI with `claude -p` plus `--output-format json --json-schema`, prompting: "Find any hardcoded secrets in this diff." Each week the job reports about 300 findings, and 94% of them are test fixtures that use documented test-key prefixes such as `sk_test_`, placeholder values in `.env.example`, and sample tokens in `docs/`. Developers now routinely bypass the check. Last quarter, however, the same scan caught two real live keys in application code, so the category has to stay. Which change most effectively restores precision?
options: Rewrite the prompt to report hardcoded credentials in application code, and explicitly skip known test-key prefixes, `*.example` files and documentation samples.
Add "ignore anything that is obviously test data" to the prompt, so the model uses its own judgment to tell real secrets from fake ones.
Add few-shot examples of the real keys leaked in past incidents, so the model learns what a genuine secret looks like in this codebase.
Report only the findings whose self-assessed confidence is above 0.9, and drop every lower-confidence finding from the JSON output.
questions.why_correct: El criterio actual ('cualquier secreto') no tiene frontera. Definir qué entra (credenciales en código de aplicación) y qué se saltea (prefijos de test documentados, `*.example`, docs) elimina el ruido sin apagar una categoría que ya atrapó claves reales.

why_wrong.1: 'Obviamente de test' es vago: el modelo ya creía que esos fixtures eran secretos.
why_wrong.2: Ayuda a reconocer secretos reales, pero no dice qué excluir: un `sk_test_` se sigue pareciendo a una clave.
why_wrong.3: La guía marca que 'solo alta confianza' no mejora la precisión frente a criterios categóricos; y un `sk_test_` puede salir con confianza alta.

questions.rule: Precisión baja en una categoría necesaria → criterios explícitos de qué entra y qué se saltea, no 'confianza'.
questions.source_quote: How general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria

questions.scenario: An electronics retailer's support agent can auto-approve refunds in the "damaged on arrival" category; every other category goes to a human. The $500 ceiling for auto-approval is already enforced by a programmatic check before the refund tool runs. The system prompt says: "Auto-approve refunds for damaged items." A weekly audit shows that 14% of auto-approvals were not damage at all: late deliveries, wrong sizes, or buyer's remorse described as "it's useless to me." Meanwhile, some clear damage cases with photos were sent to humans. What is the most effective change?
options: Ask the agent to rate its confidence that the item was damaged from 1 to 10, and auto-approve only when that score is 8 or higher.
Deploy a separate image classifier that checks the customer's photos for visible damage before the agent is allowed to approve a refund.
Change the instruction to "Auto-approve only clear damage cases and be conservative," so borderline cases get routed to a human agent.
Define damage explicitly (a physical defect shown in a photo or described specifically), list exclusions such as late delivery and wrong size, and add borderline few-shot examples.
questions.why_correct: El problema es una frontera de categoría vaga: 'dañado' se estira a todo lo que el cliente describe como malo. Definir qué es daño, listar lo que no lo es (demora, talle, arrepentimiento) y mostrar casos borde con ejemplos ataca la causa: límites de decisión poco claros.

why_wrong.0: La confianza autoinformada está mal calibrada: el agente ya está seguro en los casos que clasifica mal.
why_wrong.1: Sobreingeniería como primer paso, y no cubre los casos sin foto ni la demora descrita como daño.
why_wrong.2: 'Sé conservador' es vago: puede mandar más casos claros a humanos sin dejar de aprobar los ambiguos.

questions.rule: Categoría que se estira → definición explícita + exclusiones + few-shot de casos borde.
questions.source_quote: Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries.

questions.scenario: A platform team built an internal dependency-audit agent with the Agent SDK. For each service it lists outdated packages, known vulnerabilities from an advisory-database tool, and a license compatibility verdict (`compatible` / `incompatible`) that the legal team began relying on. A legal review of 200 verdicts found 35% were wrong, mostly on dual-licensed packages and license exceptions, while the vulnerability and version findings were accurate. Legal wants to keep receiving license information but will make compatibility decisions itself from now on. What is the most effective change to the agent's instructions?
options: Add few-shot examples of dual-licensed packages and license exceptions with the correct verdicts, so the model learns to handle the harder cases.
Explicitly exclude compatibility verdicts: report each package's license identifiers exactly as declared in its metadata, marked for legal review.
Keep the verdicts but add a disclaimer field reading "AI-generated, verify before use" to every license entry in the agent's report.
Instruct the agent to give a license verdict only when it is highly confident, and to output `unknown` for packages with dual licenses.
questions.why_correct: Es una categoría donde el agente no es confiable (35% de error) y legal igual quiere decidir. Excluirla explícitamente y reemplazarla por un dato verificable (el identificador de licencia tal como figura en la metadata) evita hallazgos poco confiables y conserva la información útil.

why_wrong.0: Mejora algo, pero sigue entregando veredictos en una categoría poco confiable que legal ya no necesita que el agente decida.
why_wrong.2: El disclaimer no vuelve correctos los veredictos: la gente los usa igual.
why_wrong.3: 'Solo si estás muy seguro' no mejora la precisión, y la confianza del modelo no coincide con dónde se equivoca (las excepciones no siempre son duales).

questions.rule: Si el modelo no es confiable en una categoría, no le pidas el veredicto: pedile el dato verificable y que decida el humano.
questions.source_quote: The impact of false positive rates on developer trust: high false positive categories undermine confidence in accurate categories

questions.scenario: A health-tech company extracts a `diagnoses` array from hospital discharge summaries to populate a clinical registry. The prompt says "List the patient's diagnoses." Clinicians auditing 400 records found that 27% of items should not be there: "rule out pneumonia", "no evidence of DVT", "family history of diabetes", "possible early sepsis, to be confirmed", and resolved conditions from the past medical history. The registry must contain only confirmed, current diagnoses for this admission. Summaries vary widely in structure across 12 hospitals, and some confirmed diagnoses appear only in the free-text narrative. What is the most effective change?
options: Pre-process each summary to keep only the section titled "Discharge diagnoses", and extract the list from that section alone.
Add a `confidence` field to each diagnosis and keep only items above 0.85, so uncertain mentions like "possible sepsis" get dropped.
Change the instruction to "List only the clinically significant diagnoses", so minor and uncertain mentions are left out of the array.
Define inclusion (confirmed and current for this admission) and exclusion (negated, ruled out, suspected, family history, resolved), with few-shot examples of each excluded type.
questions.why_correct: 'Los diagnósticos' es una frontera vaga: el modelo mete todo lo que nombra una enfermedad. Definir qué entra (confirmado y actual) y qué queda afuera (negado, descartado, sospechado, antecedente familiar, resuelto), con un ejemplo de cada exclusión, fija el límite y funciona aunque el diagnóstico esté en el texto libre.

why_wrong.0: Con 12 hospitales y estructuras distintas, muchas notas no tienen esa sección, y algunos diagnósticos confirmados están solo en el texto libre: perdés recall.
why_wrong.1: Un 'rule out pneumonia' puede salir con confianza alta: la confianza no dice si el diagnóstico está confirmado.
why_wrong.2: 'Clínicamente significativos' es otro criterio vago: una sospecha de sepsis es muy significativa y seguiría entrando.

questions.rule: Extracción que mezcla lo confirmado con lo negado o hipotético → criterios explícitos de inclusión y exclusión + ejemplos de cada exclusión.
questions.source_quote: The importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions
